---
title: "Uncertainty propagation test bed"
output: html_document
---

This exploratory test bed checks whether `propagate` can handle a simple
piece of the planned pipeline uncertainty calculation: a mean of sequential
injections corrected with one shared linear calibration. The slope and
intercept are drawn jointly from their fitted covariance matrix, so their
correlation is retained and the same calibration uncertainty applies to the
whole replicate mean.

This is a synthetic example, not a validated uncertainty model for any
instrument. The injection uncertainty below is specified for demonstration;
it should eventually be replaced by external precision estimated from
sequences of control-material injections.

```{r setup}
if (!requireNamespace("propagate", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install the optional CRAN package 'propagate' to run this test bed.")
}
```

## Fit a scale calibration

The reference values are regressed on measured standard values, matching the
scale calibration direction used by the pipeline. The fit's coefficient
covariance is retained for joint draws of intercept and slope.

```{r calibration}
calibration_standards <- data.frame(
  measured = c(-28.2, -19.7, -10.4, -1.1),
  reference = c(-28.0, -19.5, -10.0, -0.8)
)

scale_fit <- stats::lm(reference ~ measured, data = calibration_standards)
coef(scale_fit)
stats::vcov(scale_fit)
```

## Propagate uncertainty for a sequential replicate mean

The sample has three sequential injections. The uncertainty assigned to
`measured_mean` is an illustrative external precision estimate for the mean
of a three-injection sequence. It is supplied directly, rather than derived
by dividing single-injection SD by the square root of three. The
intercept and slope are represented by their fitted covariance matrix. They
are shared calibration parameters, so the calibration contribution is drawn
once for the mean rather than independently for each injection.

```{r propagate}
sample_injections <- c(-18.3, -18.0, -18.2)
measured_mean <- mean(sample_injections)
u_measured_mean <- 0.12 # illustrative SD of means from 3-injection sequences

fit_coef <- stats::coef(scale_fit)
fit_cov <- stats::vcov(scale_fit)
input_means <- c(
  intercept = unname(fit_coef[["(Intercept)"]]),
  slope = unname(fit_coef[["measured"]]),
  measured_mean = measured_mean
)

input_cov <- matrix(
  0,
  nrow = length(input_means),
  ncol = length(input_means),
  dimnames = list(names(input_means), names(input_means))
)
input_cov[c("intercept", "slope"), c("intercept", "slope")] <- fit_cov
input_cov["measured_mean", "measured_mean"] <- u_measured_mean^2

input_data <- rbind(
  mean = input_means,
  standard_uncertainty = sqrt(diag(input_cov))
)

set.seed(20261019)
mc_result <- propagate::propagate(
  expr = expression(intercept + slope * measured_mean),
  data = input_data,
  type = "stat",
  cov = input_cov,
  nsim = 100000,
  alpha = 0.05,
  check = FALSE # Skip Copula-margin fitting diagnostics for summary inputs.
)

mc_result$sim
```

## Compare with first-order propagation

For this linear correction, first-order covariance propagation has a closed
form. Agreement with the Monte Carlo standard deviation is a useful sanity
check on the package call and on the covariance wiring. Nonlinear correction
chains will need their own validation.

```{r comparison}
gradient <- c(
  intercept = 1,
  slope = measured_mean,
  measured_mean = unname(fit_coef[["measured"]])
)
u_first_order <- sqrt(
  drop(t(gradient) %*% input_cov %*% gradient)
)

comparison <- data.frame(
  method = c("First-order covariance", "propagate Monte Carlo"),
  standard_uncertainty = c(u_first_order, unname(mc_result$sim[[2]]))
)
comparison
```

The Monte Carlo result should be close to the first-order result for this
linear example, with small differences from simulation error. This example
does not yet include reference-material uncertainty, calibration residual
scatter, blank/drift/linearity corrections, or uncertainty in the plotted
x-axis.

## Synthetic correction-chain test bed

The examples below extend the test bed to the corrections used by the
pipelines. The data and uncertainty values are illustrative. EA blank
correction, GB drift correction, and GC external-standard/NACME correction
are kept as separate instrument paths; combining them into one chain would
not describe an actual experiment. Each Monte Carlo iteration draws a shared
calibration quantity once and applies it to every affected sample. It then
fits the final plotted slope, so common calibration effects and covariance
between plotted points are retained.

```{r simulation-helper}
# Draw jointly from a multivariate normal using only base R.
draw_mvn <- function(n, mu, covariance) {
  decomposition <- eigen(covariance, symmetric = TRUE)
  if (any(decomposition$values < -1e-10)) {
    stop("Covariance matrix is not positive semidefinite.")
  }
  roots <- decomposition$vectors %*%
    diag(sqrt(pmax(decomposition$values, 0)), nrow = length(mu))
  sweep(matrix(stats::rnorm(n * length(mu)), nrow = n) %*% t(roots),
        2, mu, `+`)
}

summarize_slope_draws <- function(draws) {
  stats::quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

### GC: shared date offsets and NACME correction

This models the experiment's additive external-standard offset and the
carbon-balance NACME correction. The external offset is shared by samples on
the same date. The NACME estimate is shared by samples of the same compound
and date. The example treats the supplied uncertainties as standard
uncertainties; in a real run they should come from sequential standard
injections and the reference-material certificate.

```{r gc-offset-nacme}
set.seed(20261020)
n_mc <- 20000L

gc_samples <- data.frame(
  treatment = 1:6,
  correction_date = rep(as.Date(c("2026-09-14", "2026-09-15")), each = 3),
  compound_id = "AA1",
  measured_mean = c(-19.2, -18.8, -18.3, -18.0, -17.7, -17.1),
  u_measured_mean = rep(0.10, 6)
)

# Illustrative standard uncertainties for each shared calibration estimate.
gc_daily_offset <- data.frame(
  correction_date = as.Date(c("2026-09-14", "2026-09-15")),
  mean = c(0.24, 0.31),
  u = c(0.12, 0.20)
)
gc_nacme <- data.frame(
  correction_date = as.Date(c("2026-09-14", "2026-09-15")),
  compound_id = "AA1",
  delta_derivatized_mean = c(-22.0, -21.7),
  u_delta_derivatized_mean = c(0.30, 0.45),
  AA_C_count = 6,
  NACME_C_count = 1,
  delta_known = -18.0,
  u_delta_known = 0.15
)

gc_slope_draws <- replicate(n_mc, {
  offset_draw <- stats::rnorm(nrow(gc_daily_offset),
                              gc_daily_offset$mean, gc_daily_offset$u)
  # The certified AA value is one shared input across both dates.
  known_draw <- stats::rnorm(1, gc_nacme$delta_known[[1]],
                             gc_nacme$u_delta_known[[1]])
  derivatized_draw <- stats::rnorm(
    nrow(gc_nacme), gc_nacme$delta_derivatized_mean,
    gc_nacme$u_delta_derivatized_mean
  )
  total_C_cal <- gc_nacme$AA_C_count + gc_nacme$NACME_C_count
  nacme_draw <- (total_C_cal * derivatized_draw -
                   gc_nacme$AA_C_count * known_draw) /
    gc_nacme$NACME_C_count
  measured_draw <- stats::rnorm(nrow(gc_samples),
                                gc_samples$measured_mean,
                                gc_samples$u_measured_mean)

  date_index <- match(gc_samples$correction_date,
                      gc_daily_offset$correction_date)
  nacme_index <- match(gc_samples$correction_date,
                       gc_nacme$correction_date)
  externally_corrected <- measured_draw + offset_draw[date_index]
  total_C <- gc_nacme$AA_C_count[nacme_index] +
    gc_nacme$NACME_C_count[nacme_index]
  final_delta <- (total_C * externally_corrected -
                    gc_nacme$NACME_C_count[nacme_index] *
                    nacme_draw[nacme_index]) /
    gc_nacme$AA_C_count[nacme_index]
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(final_delta ~ gc_samples$treatment))[[2]])
})

summarize_slope_draws(gc_slope_draws)
```

### EA: blank area-subtraction correction

For EA, blank area and blank isotope value enter the nonlinear correction
formula. This example draws the blank means and the sample injection means,
applies the correction, and refits the plotted slope in every iteration.
Blank-mean uncertainties here use SD divided by square root of the blank
count as a simple starting assumption; check that assumption against the
actual blank sequence and any run structure.

```{r ea-blank}
set.seed(20261021)
ea_samples <- data.frame(
  treatment = 1:6,
  area = c(900, 950, 1000, 1050, 1100, 1150),
  measured_mean = c(-26.0, -24.8, -24.1, -22.9, -21.8, -20.9),
  u_measured_mean = rep(0.12, 6)
)
blank_area <- 45
blank_area_sd <- 6
blank_delta <- -28.0
blank_delta_sd <- 0.8
n_blanks <- 8

ea_slope_draws <- replicate(n_mc, {
  area_blank_draw <- stats::rnorm(1, blank_area,
                                  blank_area_sd / sqrt(n_blanks))
  delta_blank_draw <- stats::rnorm(1, blank_delta,
                                   blank_delta_sd / sqrt(n_blanks))
  measured_draw <- stats::rnorm(nrow(ea_samples),
                                ea_samples$measured_mean,
                                ea_samples$u_measured_mean)
  corrected <- (ea_samples$area * measured_draw -
                  area_blank_draw * delta_blank_draw) /
    (ea_samples$area - area_blank_draw)
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(corrected ~ ea_samples$treatment))[[2]])
})

summarize_slope_draws(ea_slope_draws)
```

### GB: drift-model coefficient covariance

The drift fit is based on one mean per standard analysis. Drawing its
intercept and slope jointly from the fitted covariance matrix preserves their
correlation. The fitted drift correction is shared by samples at the same
analysis number. This example adds a sample-mean precision term and refits
the final slope for each draw.

```{r gb-drift}
set.seed(20261022)
drift_standards <- data.frame(
  analysis_no = c(1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16),
  mean_delta = c(-21.1, -20.9, -20.8, -20.5, -20.4, -20.1)
)
drift_fit <- stats::lm(mean_delta ~ analysis_no, data = drift_standards)
drift_coef_names <- c("(Intercept)", "analysis_no")
drift_coef_mean <- stats::coef(drift_fit)[drift_coef_names]
drift_coef_cov <- stats::vcov(drift_fit)[drift_coef_names, drift_coef_names]
drift_reference_analysis <- mean(drift_standards$analysis_no)

gb_samples <- data.frame(
  treatment = 1:6,
  analysis_no = c(2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17),
  measured_mean = c(-22.0, -21.5, -21.2, -20.6, -20.0, -19.7),
  u_measured_mean = rep(0.10, 6)
)

gb_slope_draws <- replicate(n_mc, {
  coef_draw <- setNames(
    as.numeric(draw_mvn(1, drift_coef_mean, drift_coef_cov)[1, ]),
    drift_coef_names
  )
  measured_draw <- stats::rnorm(nrow(gb_samples),
                                gb_samples$measured_mean,
                                gb_samples$u_measured_mean)
  sample_fit <- coef_draw[["(Intercept)"]] +
    coef_draw[["analysis_no"]] * gb_samples$analysis_no
  reference_fit <- coef_draw[["(Intercept)"]] +
    coef_draw[["analysis_no"]] * drift_reference_analysis
  drift_corrected <- measured_draw - (sample_fit - reference_fit)
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(drift_corrected ~ gb_samples$treatment))[[2]])
})

summarize_slope_draws(gb_slope_draws)
```

These examples estimate uncertainty on the *plotted slope*, not just on
individual corrected values. They assume independent sample-mean errors and
normal draws for the listed calibration quantities. In the next step, replace
the illustrative inputs with the run's sequential control-standard means,
reference uncertainties, blanks, and sample replicate summaries; then compare
the Monte Carlo results against analytical propagation for cases where a
closed-form result is available.
